name: The Aztec Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Aztec Empire: From Huey Tlatoani to Enslaved
period: 1428–1521 (from the Triple Alliance to the Spanish conquest)

tiers.name: The huey tlatoani
tiers.you: You command the armies of the Triple Alliance, receive the tribute of its provinces and lead the worship of Huitzilopochtli, but the lords who chose you expect victories, and one of your predecessors was probably murdered by his own court.
tiers.kid: The huey tlatoani, or “great speaker”, ruled the Aztecs from the island city of Tenochtitlan.
tiers.rise: Each ruler was chosen by the lords from the close kin of earlier rulers, a brother, son, nephew or grandson who had proved himself in war. He could also be removed: in 1520 the council of Tenochtitlan deposed Moctezuma II, then a captive of the Spaniards, and chose his brother Cuitláhuac.
tiers.why: At the top stood the huey tlatoani, the “great speaker”.

tiers.name: Nobles
tiers.you: You were born a noble: you live on tribute and the labour of commoners, wear fine garments forbidden to others, and were schooled at the calmecac for war, office or the priesthood.
tiers.kid: Aztec nobles were born into their rank, went to temple schools and became generals, officials and priests.
tiers.rise: Rank came by birth, and a lesser noble who married a daughter of a grander lineage passed her higher standing to their children. A commoner could enter the nobility only by outstanding deeds, and then only for his own lifetime; a noble who disgraced himself could be cast down among the commoners.
tiers.why: The nobles (pipiltin) were born to their rank and claimed descent from the Toltecs and, through them, from the god Quetzalcoatl.

tiers.name: Priests
tiers.you: You serve a god in one of the temples, keep long vigils and fasts, draw your own blood in penance and teach the boys of the temple school.
tiers.kid: Aztec priests looked after the temples, taught in the schools and led the festivals for the gods.
tiers.rise: Parents chose a boy’s school at his birth, and future priests trained in the temple schools. It brought a commoner respect, but historians doubt it was a quick road to high rank.
tiers.why: Priests (teopixqui, “keepers of the god”) served the gods in the great temples and in the temple of every calpolli.

tiers.name: Long-distance merchants and luxury craftsmen
tiers.you: You lead trading expeditions beyond the empire’s frontiers, report what you see to the ruler, and keep your wealth hidden so as not to provoke the envy of the nobles.
tiers.kid: Aztec merchants made long journeys to faraway lands to trade for colourful feathers and other treasures.
tiers.rise: Membership passed from father to son, and a newcomer needed the consent of the guild and the approval of its lord.
tiers.why: The pochteca were professional long-distance merchants, organised in hereditary guilds in thirteen towns of the Valley of Mexico, each with its own ward, temple, leaders and laws, and with their own god, Yacatecuhtli.

tiers.name: Commoners
tiers.you: You farm your household’s plot of calpolli land, pay tribute in cloth and labour, and train for war in the hope of winning honour by taking captives.
tiers.kid: Most Aztecs were farmers who grew maize, beans and squash and gave part of what they made to their rulers.
tiers.rise: A youth who took a captive became a full warrior, and one who took four could join the eagle or jaguar warriors and be made a quauhpilli, a noble for life but not by descent; Moctezuma II made this harder. Debt, crime or famine could push a family into slavery.
tiers.why: Most people were commoners (macehualtin), organised in calpolli: wards or villages of related families, each with its own leader, temple and school.

tiers.name: Landless tenants
tiers.you: You farm land that belongs to a noble lord and owe him part of your harvest and your labour; your plot depends on him, not on a calpolli.
tiers.kid: Some Aztec farmers had no land of their own and worked the fields of a noble instead.
tiers.rise: On colonial accounts the status passed from parents to children with the land. Like any commoner, a tenant’s son could win honour and rank by taking captives in war.
tiers.why: Not every commoner belonged to a calpolli with land of its own.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to a master, perhaps because you sold yourself to pay a debt; you may marry and keep property of your own, and your children will be born free.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people had to work for an owner without pay, but their children were born free.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by working off the debt, by the owner’s gift or will, since owners often freed loyal slaves at their death, or by escape to the palace or a temple. Whatever happened, a slave’s children were born free.
tiers.why: Enslaved people (tlacotin) were owned by others, but Aztec slavery was not inherited: the children of slaves were born free.
